text: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, also known as the Amritsar massacre, occurred on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, Punjab, British India. A large crowd had gathered at the Jallianwala Bagh during the annual Baisakhi fair to protest against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of pro-Indian independence activists Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal. In response, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer surrounded the crowd with Gurkha and Sikh infantrymen of the Indian Army. The Jallianwala Bagh had only one exit, with the other three sides enclosed by buildings, and Dyer blocked the exit with his troops before ordering them to open fire on the crowd, continuing to shoot even as people tried to flee. Firing lasted approximately ten minutes until ammunition was low and troops were ordered to stop. Estimates of the dead range from 379 to 1,500 or more, with over 1,200 injured, of whom 192 sustained serious injuries. Britain has never formally apologised for the massacre, though it expressed deep "regret" in 2019. The event led to a re-evaluation by the Imperial British military of its use of force against civilians, adopting a policy of "minimal force whenever possible," although this was not consistently followed, especially during later actions like the Mau Mau rebellion. The brutality and lack of accountability shocked the nation, leading to a loss of faith in British intentions and condemnation by Winston Churchill, who called the action "unutterably monstrous." In the UK House of Commons on 8 July 1920, members voted 247 to 37 against Dyer. The ineffective inquiry and initial praise for Dyer fueled widespread anger among Indians, contributing to the non-cooperation movement of 1920–22. During World War I, British India contributed heavily with soldiers and resources, but the war's costs—high casualties, inflation, heavy taxation, the 1918 flu pandemic, and trade disruption—exacerbated suffering. This context revived nationalist sentiment, leading to the Lucknow Pact in 1916 and the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms in 1917, though these were seen as insufficient. Mahatma Gandhi emerged as a leading figure, and civil disobedience grew. The Ghadar conspiracy, which was thwarted by British intelligence, and the presence of Raja Mahendra Pratap’s Kabul mission, along with ongoing revolutionary activity in Punjab and Bengal, led to the formation of a sedition committee in 1918 chaired by Sidney Rowlatt. The committee's recommendations resulted in the passage of the Rowlatt Act in 1919, which extended the Defence of India Act 1915 to limit civil liberties. The Act caused widespread unrest, prompting Muhammad Ali Jinnah to resign from his Bombay seat, stating that a government passing such a law in peacetime forfeited its claim to be civilised. Gandhi’s call for protest against the Rowlatt Act triggered massive unrest, especially in Punjab, where rail, telegraph, and communication systems were disrupted. The British Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab, Michael O'Dwyer, believed the gatherings were early signs of a coordinated revolt planned for May, similar to the 1857 revolt. Some historians, including James Houssemayne Du Boulay, argue the massacre was a deliberate response to fears of a Ghadarite uprising. On 10 April, a protest at Miles Irving’s residence to demand the release of Satyapal and Kitchlew ended with a military picket killing several protesters and sparking riots, including arson attacks on British banks and assaults on two British women. On 11 April, Marcella Sherwood, an English missionary, was attacked by a mob while trying to evacuate children from her school; she was rescued by local Indians and hidden at Gobindgarh Fort. Dyer, angered by the assault, ordered Indian men to crawl on their hands and knees through the Kucha Kurrichhan street, claiming it was to show that a British woman was as sacred as a Hindu god. He also authorised public whippings of those near police officers. Sherwood later defended Dyer, calling him "the saviour of the Punjab." For two days, Amritsar remained quiet, but violence continued elsewhere in Punjab, with railway lines cut, telegraph posts destroyed, government buildings burned, and three Europeans killed. By 13 April, martial law was imposed in Punjab, banning gatherings of more than four people. On 12 April, leaders of a hartal met at the Hindu College–Dhab Khatikan to plan a protest at 16:30 in the Jallianwala Bagh, organised by Muhammad Bashir and chaired by Lal Kanhyalal Bhatia, with resolutions against the Rowlatt Act, British actions, and the detention of Satyapal and Kitchlew. On 13 April, Dyer banned all meetings, a notice not widely disseminated, and the crowd gathered peacefully to celebrate Baisakhi and protest the arrests. At 09:00, Dyer announced a pass system, a curfew from 20:00, and a ban on public meetings. The proclamation was read in English, Urdu, Hindi, and Punjabi, but many ignored it. Local police learned of the meeting through word of mouth and informants. Dyer was informed at 12:40 and returned to his base at 13:30. By mid-afternoon, thousands had gathered in the Jallianwala Bagh, an open area of 6–7 acres (2.4–2.8 ha) surrounded by walls about 10 feet (3.0 m) high, with five narrow entrances, several with lockable gates. The crowd included pilgrims, farmers, traders, and merchants who had come to the Baisakhi fair. Dyer used an aeroplane to estimate the crowd size at about 6,000, though the Hunter Commission estimated between 10,000 and 20,000. Dyer and Deputy Commissioner Miles Irving took no action to disperse the crowd peacefully, a serious criticism later levelled at both. An hour after the meeting began at 17:30, Dyer arrived with 50 armed troops, all equipped with .303 Lee–Enfield rifles, and two armoured cars with machine guns. The vehicles could not enter through the narrow entrances. Dyer ordered his troops to block the main exits and begin firing at the densest sections of the crowd, where people were trying to flee. Firing continued for about ten minutes, with unarmed civilians—including men, women, elderly people, and children—killed. A cease-fire was ordered after about one-third of the ammunition was used. Dyer later claimed the purpose was "not to disperse the meeting but to punish the Indians for disobedience." The next day, he reported that between 200 and 300 were killed and that his party fired 1,650 rounds. In addition to direct deaths, many died in stampedes at the narrow gates or by jumping into the well in the center of the Bagh, which measured about 20 feet (6.1 m) in diameter. A plaque placed after independence states that 120 bodies were removed from the well. Dyer imposed an early curfew, preventing wounded people from being moved and leading to many deaths from their injuries. The number of casualties is disputed. Initial reports cited 200 casualties, a figure later acknowledged by the Government of Punjab and a senior civil servant, who admitted the actual number could be higher. The Sewa Samiti reported 379 deaths and 192 seriously wounded. The Hunter Commission concluded 379 deaths and approximately 1,500 injured. At a meeting of the Imperial Legislative Council on 12 September 1919, Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya reported that 42 boys were among the dead, the youngest only 7 months old. The Hunter Commission confirmed 337 men, 41 boys, and a six-week-old baby were killed. In July 1919, officials invited residents to report deaths, but the information was incomplete due to fear of identification and lack of close family ties. Winston Churchill reported nearly 400 killed and three or four times that number wounded to Parliament on 8 July 1920. Due to flawed official figures on crowd size (6,000–20,000), rounds fired, and duration of shooting, the Indian National Congress conducted its own inquiry, concluding over 1,500 casualties, with approximately 1,000 killed. Swami Shraddhanand wrote to Gandhi that 1,500 people died. Reginald Dyer, the British military officer responsible for the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919, reported to his superiors that he had been "confronted by a revolutionary army," to which Major General William Beynon replied via telegram: "Your action correct and Lieutenant Governor approves." O'Dwyer requested martial law be imposed in Amritsar and other areas, which was granted by Viceroy Lord Chelmsford. Thousands were detained in the days following the massacre, with historian Harish Puri noting at least 115 people killed by security forces after 13 April. Winston Churchill, in a speech to the House of Commons on 8 July 1920, reported nearly 400 killed and three or four times that number wounded, describing the crowd as unarmed, pinned in a narrow space with few exits, and subjected to sustained gunfire for 8 to 10 minutes until ammunition was exhausted. The official British figures were widely considered flawed, as the crowd size was estimated between 6,000 and 20,000, and the Indian National Congress conducted its own inquiry, concluding over 1,500 deaths with approximately 1,000 killed. Swami Shraddhanand informed Gandhi of 1,500 deaths. The British Government attempted to suppress information about the massacre, but news spread in India, leading to widespread outrage; details only became known in Britain by December 1919. The event caused many moderate Indians to abandon loyalty to the British and become nationalists distrustful of British rule. The Hunter Commission, established on 14 October 1919 under William, Lord Hunter, was tasked with investigating disturbances in Bombay, Delhi, and Punjab, and held its official sittings at the Lahore Town Hall. After meeting in New Delhi on 29 October, the commission gathered witness statements in Delhi, Ahmedabad, Bombay, and Lahore, conducting rigorous cross-examination despite not being a formal court. Dyer appeared before the commission on 19 November, refusing legal representation and stating he had intended to open fire if a crowd was present, believing the crowd was composed of "rebels" attempting to isolate his forces. He claimed he could have dispersed the crowd without firing but would have been ridiculed, and that he continued shooting until ammunition was nearly exhausted, refusing to tend to the wounded. The commission's final report, released on 8 March 1920, unanimously condemned Dyer's actions, calling his prolonged firing a grave error, though dissenting members argued that martial law was unjustified and there was no rebellion. The commission did not impose disciplinary action because Dyer's actions were condoned by superiors, and the Viceroy's Executive Council decided against prosecution due to political reasons, though Dyer was relieved of command on 23 March 1920 and his CBE recommendation was cancelled. He was removed from his appointment, passed over for promotion, and barred from future employment in India, dying in 1927. British authorities awarded compensation to European subjects after the massacre, and Indian subjects later demanded equal compensation and a statement of regret, leading to over 700 claims settled by 1922, with less than half the amount paid to Indian families compared to European recipients. On 13 March 1940, Udham Singh, an Indian independence activist who had been wounded at Amritsar, shot and killed Michael O'Dwyer, the lieutenant-governor who had approved Dyer's actions and was seen as the main planner. The nationalist newspaper Amrita Bazar Patrika supported the killing, and the public and revolutionaries hailed Singh as a "fighter for freedom," with The Times calling it "an expression of the pent-up fury of the down-trodden Indian People." In fascist countries, the incident was used in anti-British propaganda, with publications like Bergeret and the Berliner Börsen Zeitung praising Singh's action as courageous and the "torch of Indian freedom." At public meetings, including one in Cawnpore, people expressed that an insult to the nation had been avenged, and the Amrita Bazar Patrika stated O'Dwyer's name was linked to events India would never forget. Singh, at his trial, stated he killed O'Dwyer because he had a grudge, believed he was the real culprit, and had been trying to avenge his people for 21 years, saying he was dying for his country. He was hanged on 31 July 1940, and although figures like Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi condemned the murder as senseless, Nehru later honoured Singh in 1952, stating he saluted Udham Singh with reverence as a martyr for freedom, and Singh was thereafter given the title Shaheed. A trust founded in 1920 to build a memorial at the site, which purchased land in 1923, erected a memorial designed by Benjamin Polk, inaugurated by President Rajendra Prasad on 13 April 1961, in the presence of Jawaharlal Nehru and other leaders, with a flame later added. The bullet marks remain on the walls and adjacent buildings, and the well where people jumped to escape bullets is a protected monument. Shortly after the massacre, the official Sikh clergy of the Harmandir Sahib conferred the Saropa upon Dyer, sending shockwaves through the Sikh community. On 12 October 1920, students and faculty of Amritsar Khalsa College held a meeting to strengthen the nationalist movement, leading to the formation of the Shiromani Gurudwara Prabhandak Committee on 15 November 1920. Queen Elizabeth II did not comment on the incident during her 1961 and 1983 state visits but spoke about it at a state banquet in India on 13 October 1997, stating that Jallianwala Bagh was a distressing example of difficult episodes in British history, emphasizing that history cannot be rewritten and that lessons must be learned from its sadness. While some Indians welcomed her expression of regret, others criticized it as insufficient for an apology.

On 12 October 1920, students and faculty of Amritsar Khalsa College held a meeting to strengthen the Nationalistic Movement, leading to the students advocating for an anti-British movement and the subsequent formation of the Shiromani Gurudwara Prabhandak Committee on 15 November 1920 to manage and implement reforms in Sikh shrines. Although Queen Elizabeth II did not comment on the incident during her state visits in 1961 and 1983, she spoke about it at a state banquet in India on 13 October 1997, stating that there had been difficult episodes in history, such as Jallianwala Bagh, which she said was distressing, and emphasizing that history has both moments of sadness and gladness, and that one must learn from sadness and build on gladness. While some Indians welcomed her expression of regret and sadness, others criticized it as insufficient for an apology. Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral defended the Queen, noting she had not been born at the time of the events and thus should not be required to apologize. On 14 October 1997, the Queen visited Jallianwala Bagh, paying her respects with a 30-second moment of silence, wearing a dress described as pink apricot or saffron—of religious significance to Hindus and Sikhs and one of the colors on India's flag—and removed her shoes, laying a wreath of marigolds. During the visit, protests occurred in Amritsar with people waving black flags and chanting "Queen, go back," and although the Queen and Prince Philip signed the visitor's book, their failure to offer any comment regretting the incident drew criticism. During the visit, Philip and his guide Partha Sarathi Mukherjee came upon a plaque stating that "about two thousand Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims ... were martyred in a non-violent struggle," to which Philip responded, "That's a bit exaggerated," adding, "it must include the wounded," and claimed he had learned this from General Dyer's son, whom he met while in the Navy. These remarks drew widespread condemnation in India, with Indian journalist Praveen Swami writing in Frontline that Philip's comment suggested the death of 379 people was inadequate to appall the royal conscience and revealed a lack of integrity in the wreath-laying. There have been long-standing demands in India for Britain to apologize for the massacre. Winston Churchill, on 8 July 1920, urged the House of Commons to punish Dyer, describing the massacre as "monstrous," and succeeded in persuading the House to forcibly retire Dyer, though he preferred disciplinary action. A statement by Sir William Vincent, the home member of the Viceroy's Council, expressed deep regret, declaring that "overdrastic and severe action, excessive use of force and acts ... reasonably interpreted as designed to humiliate Indian people ... cannot but be regarded as unpardonable (and) morally indefensible," and the Indian Government reported to the UK that Dyer's actions were beyond what was necessary and violated the principle of using reasonable and minimum force. A manual was created afterward to instruct officers on the use of force, to be applied only when absolutely necessary. In February 2013, David Cameron became the first serving British prime minister to visit the site, laying a wreath and describing the Amritsar massacre as "a deeply shameful event in British history, one that Winston Churchill rightly described at that time as monstrous," adding that the UK must never forget what happened and must stand up for the right of peaceful protests; he did not deliver an official apology, which drew criticism, including from Sankarshan Thakur of The Telegraph, who noted that British leaders had long avoided using the word "sorry." The issue resurfaced during Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge's 2016 visit to India, when both skipped the memorial site. In 2017, Indian author and politician Shashi Tharoor suggested that the Jallianwala Bagh centenary in 2019 could be a "good time" for Britain to apologize for wrongs during colonial rule. On 6 December 2017, London's mayor Sadiq Khan called on the British government to apologize. In February 2019, the British House of Lords began debating the massacre. On 12 April 2019, a ceremony was held in Amritsar just before the centenary anniversary, where Prime Minister Theresa May called the 1919 shooting of unarmed civilians a "shameful scar," echoing David Cameron's 2013 statement. On 15 April 2019, a national memorial event titled "Jallianwala Bagh 100 Years On" was held in the British Parliament, hosted by Jasvir Singh and organized by City Sikhs and the Faiths Forum for London, featuring testimonies from survivors read from the book Eyewitness at Amritsar, traditional musical performances, and a minute's silence to remember those killed a century earlier. In April 2019, The Asian Awards honored the Martyrs of Jallianwala Bagh with the Founders Award, accepted by Jagmohan Singh, the nephew of Bhagat Singh. On Christmas Day 2021, Jaswant Singh Chail entered the grounds of Windsor Castle where Queen Elizabeth II was living, intending to assassinate her with a crossbow; in a video posted to Snapchat, he stated, "This is revenge for those who have died in the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre. It is also revenge for those who have been killed, humiliated and discriminated on because of their race." He was arrested before entering the castle and in February 2023 admitted three counts of treason, the first such charge in the UK since 1981. In a televised hearing, Mr Justice Hilliard sentenced Chail to nine years with a further five years on extended licence, under a hybrid order, meaning he will be transferred from Broadmoor psychiatric hospital to serve his sentence in prison when he is well enough. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre remains a common subject of literature and film.
